messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Bartender
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Emotion Control: I try hard to control my emotions, Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Maria is a 38-year-old bartender who has been with her partner, David, for nearly six years. She came to therapy at David’s urging, though she is not entirely sure what talking can change. What happened is over. The problem, as she sees it, is that she cannot stop seeing it.

The event itself took place eighteen months ago, on a warm October evening. Maria had just finished a double shift and was walking home through the alley behind the bar—a shortcut she had taken hundreds of times. She heard a scuffle, then a man’s voice shouting, then a wet, cracking sound. She rounded the corner and saw two men on the ground. One was on top of the other, fist raised. The man on the bottom was David. She did not see the punch land, but she heard it. She screamed, and the attacker ran. David’s face was already swelling, blood coming from his nose and a cut above his eye. Maria called 911, but in the moments before help arrived, she could not make herself touch him. She stood frozen, phone in hand, repeating his name. Later, at the hospital, the doctors said it was a concussion, a broken nose, and three fractured ribs. He healed. But Maria did not.

Her memory of that night is a strange patchwork. Some parts are impossibly vivid: the sound of the punch, the pattern of the gravel where David’s head hit the ground, the way his eyes fluttered before he lost consciousness. She can replay these images in high definition, as though they are happening in the present. Other parts are simply gone. She cannot remember dialing 911, though she knows she did. She cannot remember what she said to the paramedic. There is a blank space where those minutes should be, and she has learned not to push against it, because pushing only brings the clear images back stronger.

Maria has come to believe that what happened is her fault. She was the one who chose the shortcut. She was the one who wanted to get home faster. If she had taken the main street, David would not have been attacked. She tells herself this so often that it has become a kind of fact, as solid as her own name. And if she cannot trust her own judgment about something as simple as a route home, then how can she trust anyone else? She has started to see people differently. A customer at the bar who seems too friendly—she wonders what they are hiding. A neighbor who offers to help carry groceries—she wonders what they want in return. She has become certain that people are not what they seem, that everyone has a hidden agenda, and that relying on anyone is a mistake she will not make again.

To manage this, Maria has built a careful set of rules. She avoids the news entirely. If a television in the bar is tuned to a local station, she asks a coworker to change it. She cannot watch stories about assaults, muggings, or random violence—they feel too close, as though the screen might reach out and pull her back into that alley. She has also learned to control her emotions with fierce discipline. At work, she is professional, smiling, efficient. But the moment she feels a flicker of anger or fear, she pushes it down, locks it away. She has become an expert at appearing fine while feeling nothing at all. And she has avoided seeking any kind of help—medical or psychological—until now. David made this appointment for her, and she came because she was tired of his worry, not because she believed it would work.

The consequences have been accumulating quietly. She has stopped walking anywhere alone. She drives even the shortest distances, circling blocks for parking rather than taking a two-minute walk. At work, she has started asking a coworker to walk her to her car after every shift, even though the lot is well-lit and only fifty feet from the door. She knows this looks strange, but the alternative—standing in that dark lot by herself—is unthinkable. David has noticed, and their conversations have grown strained. He wants to go out, to see friends, to live normally. She cannot explain why she feels safest in their apartment, with the door locked and the blinds drawn.

What finally brought Maria to this chair is not insight or readiness. It is exhaustion. She is tired of the vigilance, tired of the images that play behind her eyes when she tries to sleep, tired of the way her chest tightens every time she hears a sudden noise. She does not know if therapy can help, and she is afraid that talking about it will only make the images sharper. But she is here. And for now, that is enough.
